cells.tense: The harvest has arrived, and the hands that made it are still here holding it.
cells.act: let the friction test what you are committed to
cells.ask: Take whatever you've tended longest that still carries weight, and this week stop shielding it from the hard part. See what your commitment turns out to be.
cells.core:
It comes easier now to stand under a heavy day and still notice what has grown around you. What you carried at the edge of your strength is showing its result, and you can enjoy it without making it mean anything extra. That is a body holding well, with something on it.

Choose the long-held thing that still carries weight. This week, stop shielding it from the hard part and see what your commitment actually is. It may turn out smaller than you kept saying, or sturdier, or aimed at something else. If it's right, doing will tell you; if it isn't, you'll know sooner than another season of carrying it. There may also be an afternoon where the weight simply isn't there and the fruit is — let that count as success too.
cells.sheetLine: The enduring made something and you can enjoy it.
cells.verb: enjoying what careful tending has produced
cells.place: in the body that holds under weight

cells.tense: The season ahead is being weathered long before it arrives, and the shoulders are already set.
cells.act: meet someone in the middle and go on together
cells.ask: Pick one person and one load you're still carrying by yourself, and meet them halfway this week — the same thing carried by two instead of one.
cells.core:
Where you hold what has to be held, a future that hasn't happened is being endured. The next turn gets carried before it comes, and what has already grown gets run over by the worrying. Your strength is doing double time on a day that may not arrive, and the fruit sitting right here gets missed.

Bring one person into the same load. Meet them halfway on something you keep carrying alone — not handing it over, not doing all of it, sharing the weight of one task this week. Bracing doesn't stop because someone joins; it gets shown a road down that isn't just more holding on. Then what's already grown gets held alongside you.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for a season that hasn't come yet.
cells.verb: enjoying what careful tending has produced

cells.tense: The result was named some time in the past and a door lies behind you that you haven't walked through.
cells.act: choose which star to steer by and steer
cells.ask: Choose one thing already made that you'd still like to be real, head toward it for three days without checking the alternatives, and walk as if it were decided.
cells.core:
Where you hold under weight, pressure still arrives, but the door to what you made is behind you now. You are standing with the work already done, not enjoying it, not stepping through. Some of the load is imagined — hours spent on the next turn while the yard is already full. Your body still carries well. The direction has gone somewhere else.

Take one thing from what's already grown that you'd still like to be real, name it as your heading, and walk three days by wanting it rather than by figuring. Stop checking the alternatives. If nothing you've made feels worth choosing, that itself is the first thing to look at, not another reason to stand at the door. Choosing a heading and walking is how a body running on empty gets its charge back.

cells.tense: The garden is being kept by hands whose work keeps getting filed under luck.
cells.act: release the method, not the purpose
cells.ask: When something you're tending next gets hard, keep the purpose and drop the way you've been doing it. Afterward, count that decision as yours.
cells.core:
You're holding the garden against whatever comes and filing the strain under circumstance. The endurance has already produced something, and when people say it took real work, you answer with luck. Attention is being spent by hands you keep crediting to something else. What you care about is visible from outside; you simply haven't taken the credit.

When one of the things you tend next gets hard — a delay, a person, a plan that stops working — let your way of doing it go and keep the aim. Afterward, count that decision as yours rather than circumstance. If you've truly stopped caring, letting the method go will feel like release; if you haven't, the purpose will show up in your hands, and you'll have to share the credit with yourself.
cells.sheetLine: The garden is being kept by hands you don't count.
cells.verb: enjoying what careful tending has produced
